reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it presents OneCoin as a tradable asset and demonstrates an internal sell order, claiming that 15 coins will produce 35.14 euros and a near-term Cash account credit. A separately cited U.S. Justice Department account establishes that OneCoin was marketed and sold as a fraudulent cryptocurrency and that its claimed value was internally set. The tutorial's transaction-password field is ordinary account verification, not a request to disclose credentials to the presenter; the video does not prove that the claimed cash-out occurred.

citations.quote: And in this field I put the transaction password. Then I place the button Place order
today or tomorrow you will receive your coins to the Cash account
To mine your own coins you can get potision and ...

opening.argument: The presentation uses limited, example-based language rather than promising that every viewer will profit. The speaker says, “for example” before describing a 15-coin transaction, and explains a particular account workflow: entering an amount, supplying a transaction password, and placing an order. The description likewise says viewers can see how to sell coins, which frames the material as an explanation of a process rather than a universal investment guarantee. The evidence shows a stated expected credit, but it does not establish that the creator represented the result as risk-free, guaranteed for all viewers, or independently verified. A careful judge should distinguish demonstrating a claimed exchange function from making an unconditional promise about investment returns.

citations.quote: for example € and so by selling 15 coins I will receive 35,14 €.
In this video you can see how to sell OneCoin in our internal exchange.
Your order has successfully been ready

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference argument treats the example's stated amount and timing as a guarantee, but the supplied wording describes one transaction and does not say that every viewer will receive the same result. “Today or tomorrow” follows the claimed order outcome; it does not prove that money was solicited, that the speaker guaranteed a return, or that the interface was independently validated. The password field is shown as part of completing the user's own order form, not as a request to send credentials to the presenter.

citations.quote: for example € and so by selling 15 coins I will receive 35,14 €.
Then I place the button Place order

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it an example does not neutralize the concrete value proposition: the speaker says that selling 15 coins will produce 35.14 euros, then says the coins will reach the Cash account today or tomorrow. The form also displays a transaction-password field and a Place Order control. Those details present a near-term conversion as an ordinary, functioning outcome, even though the sampled material does not independently prove that the cash was received.

citations.quote: by selling 15 coins I will receive 35,14 €.
today or tomorrow you will receive your coins to the Cash account

opening.argument: The video's primary observable function is operational instruction. The speaker introduces herself and says she will show how to sell OneCoin, then walks through selecting trading, entering the number of coins, entering a transaction password, and placing an order. The description uses the same instructional framing, saying viewers can see how to sell coins in an exchange. The screen is a structured exchange dashboard with charts, order controls, and transaction areas, consistent with a software walkthrough. Nothing in the supplied material shows the presenter asking viewers to purchase coins, join a referral network, transfer funds to her, or disclose credentials to her. The strongest grounded characterization is a tutorial demonstrating the steps of an account operation.

citations.quote: in this video I will show you how to sell your OneCoin.
here we go to ask and here we type the number of the coins we would like to sell.
In this video you can see how to sell OneCoin in our internal exchange.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference side relies on the tutorial's subject matter to infer deceptive promotion. But showing an exchange workflow is not itself a solicitation, and the supplied material contains no instruction to buy, recruit, deposit, or pay the presenter. The reference also concedes that the password is entered into the order form rather than requested from the audience. A tutorial can report a platform's claimed operation without independently certifying that claim.

citations.quote: in this video I will show you how to sell your OneCoin.
And in this field I put the transaction password.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial framing does not make the underlying message neutral. The walkthrough is specifically about selling OneCoin, assigns a euro value to a stated number of coins, and tells viewers that the proceeds will reach a Cash account shortly after the order. The interface is therefore used to demonstrate an apparent cash-out pathway, not merely generic software operation. Even without a direct request to pay the presenter, that concrete conversion claim promotes the token's supposed value.

citations.quote: I will show you how to sell your OneCoin.
by selling 15 coins I will receive 35,14 €.
today or tomorrow you will receive your coins to the Cash account

opening.argument: The supplied material depicts an ordinary order-entry transaction on an exchange interface. The visible form has conventional fields for order type, quantity, price, transaction value, fee, expiration, and password, plus a Place Order button. The speaker describes selling a stated quantity and says the resulting amount is directed to a Cash account. Whatever one thinks of the platform, the video does not show a request for a deposit, a guaranteed downline income, recruitment, or a demand that viewers surrender credentials to the presenter. It also does not show the presenter receiving money from viewers. The internal-versus-external description is inconsistent: the description says “internal exchange,” while the narration says “external exchange.” That ambiguity weakens any confident conclusion about the mechanism being promoted.

citations.quote: we have sold our coins in the external exchange
sell OneCoin in our internal exchange.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The reference argument identifies a sell order, but an order form alone does not establish a scam mechanism. The supplied frames show fields and a button, while the narration says the order was ready; they do not establish a viewer deposit, referral payout, credential transfer to the presenter, or confirmed cash receipt. The conflicting descriptions of an internal and external exchange also make the mechanism less certain than the reference asserts.

citations.quote: Your order has successfully been ready
sell OneCoin in our internal exchange.
we have sold our coins in the external exchange

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A scam mechanism need not involve the presenter personally collecting a deposit or password. The relevant claim is that OneCoin can be converted into euros through the displayed exchange. The form shows a transaction value and fee, and the speaker gives a specific 15-coin-to-35.14-euro example followed by a near-term Cash account statement. The internal/external wording changes the venue, not the central value proposition that the token can be sold for cash.
